narr: Let's explore some key dates and figures from the history of Uzbekistan during weeks 5 and 6 of our course.
We'll start with some important milestones in the country's legal and constitutional development.

events.text: Entry into force of the 2014 Protocol for Uzbekistan
Decree PF-5775: Creation of National Commission and Institute of the National Rapporteur
ILO independent monitoring: systematic child labor eliminated; issue removed from agenda in 2019

narr: Let's look at some important dates in Uzbekistan's recent legal history.
In June 2019, Uzbekistan ratified the 2014 Protocol, which then entered into force in September 2020.
Also in July 2019, President issued Decree PF-5775 establishing a National Commission and Institute of the National Rapporteur.
Between 2014 and 2018, ILO monitoring found that systematic child labor had been eliminated, leading to the issue being removed from the agenda in 2019.
Now let's examine some key numbers related to the constitutional development of Uzbekistan.

data.heading: Constitution Draft Discussion
bullets: 6,000+ proposals and 1,000+ letters submitted during nationwide discussion

narr: During the nationwide discussion of the Constitution draft, there was significant public participation.
Citizens submitted over 6,000 proposals and 1,000 letters.
As a result, 60 out of 127 articles were amended, and 4 were completely excluded.
The Constitution draft went through several iterations before its final form.
The initial draft had 158 articles, which were successively reduced to 149, then 137, and finally 127 articles.
The Constitutional Commission's composition changed from 64 to 71 members.
The working group consisted of 32 people, who organized into 6 subgroups.
Additionally, 50 researchers were involved in the process.

data.heading: December 8, 1992 Session
bullets: About 80 changes and clarifications made by deputies

narr: At the December 8, 1992 session, deputies made about 80 changes and clarifications to the draft.
This was the session where the Constitution of Uzbekistan was formally adopted.
Let's now turn our attention to the development of Uzbekistan's judicial system.

data.heading: 1938 Law on Judicial System
bullets: Law consisted of 8 chapters and 80 articles
Regional and Supreme Court judges served for 5 years

narr: The Law "On the Judicial System" of 1938 was a foundational document.
It contained 8 chapters and 80 articles.
The law specified terms of service: people's judges served for 3 years, while judges in regional and Supreme Courts served for 5 years.

data.heading: People's Courts in Uzbek SSR (1939)
bullets: 226 people's courts existed in the second half of 1939
Out of 225 people's judges, 46 were women

narr: In the second half of 1939, there were 226 people's courts in the Uzbek SSR.
Among the 225 people's judges, 46 were women, showing some gender diversity in the judiciary.
However, only 17 judges had higher education, indicating limited formal qualifications among judicial personnel.

data.heading: Judicial Personnel Changes (1937-1939)
bullets: 541 judges were dismissed during this period
Only 6 people's judges completed their full term
This represents just 2.6% of the total

narr: The period from 1937 to 1939 saw significant changes in judicial personnel.
A total of 541 judges were dismissed during this time.
Remarkably, only 6 people's judges completed their full term, which represents just 2.6% of the total.
This indicates a period of instability and purges in the judicial system.

data.heading: Impact of World War II (1942)
bullets: Staffing of regional courts decreased from 230 (1941) to 187 (1942)

narr: The impact of World War II was also felt in the judicial system.
In 1942, 28 people's courts were reduced, likely due to resource constraints.
The staffing of regional courts decreased from 230 in 1941 to 187 in 1942, showing the strain the war placed on the judicial infrastructure.
Let's now look at some modern statistics related to Uzbekistan's legal landscape and global context.
The Lex.uz database is a comprehensive legal resource.
It contains 99,706 documents in total.
Among these, there are 1,228 laws, including 6 constitutional laws and 18 codes.
The database also includes 5,749 presidential decrees, showing the significant role of executive orders in Uzbekistan's legal system.

data.heading: Global Slavery Statistics
bullets: 40.3 million people in modern slavery worldwide
Every fourth victim is a child

narr: Looking at the global context, the ILO reported in 2017 that there were 40.3 million people in modern slavery worldwide.
This includes 24.9 million people in forced labor.
Additionally, there were 15.4 million people in forced marriages.
Tragically, every fourth victim of modern slavery is a child.

data.heading: Uzbekistan's ILO Commitments
bullets: As of January 1, 2021, Uzbekistan ratified 17 ILO conventions

narr: Uzbekistan has made significant commitments to international labor standards.
As of January 1, 2021, the country had ratified 17 ILO conventions.
Among these, 8 are considered fundamental conventions.
Uzbekistan had also ratified 1 protocol related to these conventions.

data.heading: Forced Labor Cases (2019-2020)
bullets: 141 of these cases were in cotton production
42 officials held accountable for the 2020 campaign

narr: Uzbekistan has been addressing issues of forced labor.
In 2019, there were 259 documented cases of forced labor.
Notably, 141 of these cases were related to cotton production.
The fines for these cases amounted to 772 million sum.
In 2020, 42 officials were held accountable for their roles in the forced labor campaign.
